chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee', who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about vessels of gold and silver, and he disliked them. I said, 'Some of our companions have narrated that there was a silver-plated mirror belonging to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him).' He said, 'No, by God, it only had a ring of silver which is with me. Then, when al-Abbas was cured, a rod was made for him, plated with silver, similar to what is made for children, the silver of which was worth about ten dirhams. So Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) ordered it to be broken.'

key_terms.فَكَرِهَهَا: and he disliked it (indicating recommended avoidance)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on using gold and silver vessels according to Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the distinction between full gold/silver vessels and minor adornments, reinforcing the Shia jurisprudential principle of avoiding ostentation (takhalluq) in daily utensils. The Imam’s personal practice of breaking a silver-plated cane exemplifies the rigorous application of *karahat* (dislike/preference) to distinguish Islamic modesty from the luxury of the pre-Islamic and Abbasite elites. This hadith is pivotal in establishing the ruling that while not strictly forbidden, the use of pure gold and silver for eating and drinking is discouraged to maintain spiritual humility.
